title: Ambiguous Requirement
scenario: A stakeholder provides a requirement that is later interpreted differently by the development team and the customer.

requirements: The system shall load quickly.
The system shall be user-friendly.
evidence.snippet: No code provided — focus on requirement quality.

primary.question: What is the main problem with these requirements?
options: They are ambiguous and not measurable
They are written as non-functional requirements
They contain too many technical details
primary.answer: They are ambiguous and not measurable

secondary.question: What is the best improvement?
options: Rewrite using measurable criteria (e.g., seconds, error rate, satisfaction score)
Move the requirements into the code comments
Replace them with user stories only
secondary.answer: Rewrite using measurable criteria (e.g., seconds, error rate, satisfaction score)

hint: Ask yourself: could you test 'quickly' or 'user-friendly' objectively?
explanation: The wording is vague and open to interpretation. Good requirements should be clear and verifiable (testable). Rewriting with measurable targets improves precision and reduces misunderstanding.

title: Missing Security Requirement
scenario: A team designs a system to store student records. The requirements list features and performance targets but nothing about access control or data protection.

requirements: Users can view student profiles.
Users can edit student profiles.
The system must support 500 concurrent users.
evidence.snippet: The database contains names, addresses, and grades.

primary.question: What is the most serious missing requirement type?

secondary.question: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Add requirements for authentication, authorisation, and audit logging
Delay security decisions until after deployment
secondary.answer: Add requirements for authentication, authorisation, and audit logging

hint: What protects sensitive data from unauthorised users?
explanation: When handling sensitive records, security requirements are essential (authentication, authorisation, auditing, and data protection). Leaving them out is a major risk.

title: Incorrect Multiplicity
scenario: A team models a system where students submit assignments. They create a Student–Assignment relationship but users report the model doesn't reflect reality.

requirements: A student can submit multiple assignment submissions (one per assignment).
Each submission belongs to exactly one student.
evidence.snippet: No code provided — focus on the object model.

primary.question: What is wrong with the relationship shown?
options: It should be composition instead of association

secondary.question: Which corrected multiplicities best fit the requirements?

hint: Can one student submit more than one thing over time?
explanation: The requirements state multiple submissions per student. The model should represent one-to-many: a student can have zero or more submissions, while each submission has exactly one student.

title: Aggregation vs Composition
scenario: A team designs a model for an Order system. They debate whether Order 'has' OrderLines using aggregation or composition.

requirements: An Order consists of one or more OrderLines.
OrderLines should not exist without an Order.
Deleting an Order deletes its lines.
evidence.snippet: No code provided — focus on relationship semantics.

primary.question: Which relationship type best fits the requirements?

secondary.question: Why is composition more appropriate here?
options: OrderLines have the same lifecycle as Order and don’t exist independently
OrderLines must be shared between multiple Orders
OrderLines should exist even when the Order is deleted
secondary.answer: OrderLines have the same lifecycle as Order and don’t exist independently

hint: What happens to the parts when the whole is deleted?
explanation: Composition indicates strong ownership and shared lifecycle. Since OrderLines should not exist without an Order, composition fits better than aggregation.

title: Low Cohesion / High Coupling Module
scenario: A single module handles input validation, database operations, report formatting, and email notifications. Changing any feature often breaks others.

requirements: Reports must be downloadable as PDF.
Emails must be sent after actions.
Database operations must be reliable.

primary.question: What is the main design problem?
options: Low cohesion and high coupling due to too many responsibilities in one module
primary.answer: Low cohesion and high coupling due to too many responsibilities in one module

secondary.question: Which improvement is best?
options: Split into separate modules/services (validation, persistence, reporting, notifications) with clear interfaces
Add more functions to the same class to keep everything together
Move all functionality into global variables
secondary.answer: Split into separate modules/services (validation, persistence, reporting, notifications) with clear interfaces

hint: How many different reasons could this module change?
explanation: Combining unrelated responsibilities reduces cohesion and increases coupling. Splitting concerns and using clear module boundaries supports modular design and easier maintenance.

title: Verification vs Validation Confusion
scenario: A team claims the system is 'validated' because unit tests pass, but users report it doesn't meet their needs.

requirements: Users need a simple workflow with minimal steps.
The system must prevent common input mistakes.
evidence.snippet: Unit tests cover internal functions, but no user acceptance testing has been performed.

primary.question: What is the core mistake being made?
options: Confusing verification (building it right) with validation (building the right thing)
Using black-box testing instead of white-box
Testing too late in the lifecycle
primary.answer: Confusing verification (building it right) with validation (building the right thing)

secondary.question: What is the best next step to address this?
options: Perform user acceptance testing and review requirements with stakeholders
Remove all tests until the end
secondary.answer: Perform user acceptance testing and review requirements with stakeholders

hint: Unit tests show correctness of code, but do they prove it meets user needs?
explanation: Verification checks conformance to specification and correctness. Validation checks whether the product meets stakeholder needs. Both are required.

title: Conflicting Stakeholder Views
scenario: Two stakeholders disagree: one wants detailed data export features, the other wants minimal system complexity.

requirements: The system shall provide full CSV export of all user activity.
The system shall remain lightweight and simple.

secondary.question: What is the best resolution approach?

hint: Consider how requirements are prioritised when stakeholders disagree.
explanation: Conflicting stakeholder viewpoints must be negotiated and prioritised. Requirements engineering involves balancing competing needs.

title: Unbounded Loop in State Model
scenario: A state diagram allows a transition from 'Processing' back to 'Processing' without exit conditions.

primary.question: What modelling issue is present?
options: Potential infinite loop due to missing guard condition
primary.answer: Potential infinite loop due to missing guard condition

secondary.question: What is the correct improvement?
options: Add guard conditions or exit criteria to the transition
secondary.answer: Add guard conditions or exit criteria to the transition

hint: What prevents the system from staying in the same state forever?
explanation: State transitions should include clear guards or exit conditions to avoid unintended infinite loops.

title: Incorrect Use of Inheritance
scenario: A developer makes Payment inherit from User because payments are made by users.

primary.question: What is wrong with this design?
options: Inheritance is misused where association is more appropriate
primary.answer: Inheritance is misused where association is more appropriate

secondary.question: What is the better modelling choice?
options: Model Payment as associated with User
secondary.answer: Model Payment as associated with User

hint: Is a Payment a type of User?
explanation: Inheritance represents an 'is-a' relationship. A Payment is not a type of User; it is associated with a User.

title: Overly Large Sprint Commitment
scenario: A team commits to delivering 25 major features in a two-week sprint.

requirements: 25 new features planned in 14 days.

secondary.question: What is the best corrective action?
options: Re-estimate and reduce scope based on velocity
secondary.answer: Re-estimate and reduce scope based on velocity

hint: Consider agile estimation and team velocity.
explanation: Sprint planning should align with realistic team capacity. Overcommitment increases risk and technical debt.

title: Hard-Coded Security Logic
scenario: Authentication checks are hard-coded inside multiple modules instead of centralised.

primary.question: What design problem exists?
options: Security logic is tightly coupled and duplicated
primary.answer: Security logic is tightly coupled and duplicated

secondary.question: What is a better approach?
options: Centralise authentication and authorisation in a dedicated module
secondary.answer: Centralise authentication and authorisation in a dedicated module

hint: What happens when access rules change?
explanation: Duplicated security logic increases coupling and maintenance cost. Centralised control improves modularity.

title: No Regression Testing
scenario: A team fixes a bug but does not re-run previous test cases.

requirements: System must remain stable after updates.

primary.question: What is the risk?
options: New changes may break existing functionality
primary.answer: New changes may break existing functionality

hint: Think about changes affecting existing features.
explanation: Regression testing ensures that new changes do not introduce unintended side effects.

title: Uncontrolled Risk
scenario: A project identifies data migration as high risk but creates no mitigation plan.

requirements: System must migrate legacy data.

hint: Risk management involves more than identification.
explanation: Risks must be analysed and mitigation strategies defined to reduce project failure probability.

title: Incorrect Many-to-Many
scenario: A model shows Students and Courses as 1-to-1.
hint: Can a student enrol in more than one course?
explanation: Students can enrol in multiple courses, and courses contain multiple students — many-to-many.
